keyTerms.def: The science of making decisions in the presence of scarce resources; the study of how to direct resources in a way that most efficiently achieves a given goal.
A company's plan to create value in a marketplace; a plan to create and sustain a competitive advantage.
Learn how to apply economic concepts and principles to achieve superior profit performance for firms. STRAT 401 = conceptual foundations; STRAT 402 = analytical underpinnings and quantitative rigor.

Economics requires the analyst to be explicit about key elements; there is a clear linkage between conclusions and assumptions, which 'leaves an audit trail that allows one to distinguish between derived propositions and unsupported conjectures.'
'In this class, we are managers, not consumers.' (How would you feel about Netflix raising their price?)

Markets to Pursue (industry, product, geographic markets most attractive); Unique Value to Offer (cost or differentiation); Resources and Capabilities to Develop; Sustaining Advantage (barriers to imitation).

title: Industry Structure

learningObjectives.text: Know and understand the following concepts: C4 ratio, HHI
learningObjectives.src: course-data.js Session 3 'Read: Chapter 7'; S03 slides p.3

learningObjectives.text: Know how to calculate various measures of industry concentration and how they relate to market competitiveness
Understand the limitations of concentration measures

keyTerms.def: An industry is 'concentrated' when a few large firms control the industry (e.g., Auto, Airline, etc.).
Industry concentration and market competitiveness are inversely related (i.e., monopoly at 100% vs. perfect competition at ≈ 0%).
The fraction of total sales generated by the four largest firms in the industry (ranges from 0 = extremely competitive to 1 = highly concentrated).
The sum of the squared market shares of firms in a given industry multiplied by 10,000 (ranges from 0 = extremely competitive to 10,000 = monopoly).

vars.w_i: market share of firm i as a decimal

workedExamples.name: US mobile telecom 2013
workedExamples.givens: Verizon 42%, AT&T 33%, Sprint 16%, T-Mobile 3%; remaining 6% treated as one firm

workedExamples.name: Allegiant airports (Dec 2025 BTS data)
workedExamples.givens: OAK vs SFO, HOU vs IAH, MDW vs ORD shares
workedExamples.answer: OAK HHI 7,323 C4 95.4% vs SFO 2,765 / 76.8%; HOU 8,939 / 98.8% vs IAH 3,602 / 78.7%; MDW 8,632 / 99.2% vs ORD 2,503 / 78.2%. Allegiant cities are more concentrated, consistent with its strategy of avoiding competition at smaller airports.

cases: US domestic airlines 2025: C4 = 64.4%, HHI = 1,162 (S03 slides p.12)
Route-level HHIs 2025: National 1,162; LAS-LAX 1,620; ATL-MCO 5,324; LAX-SFO 2,104; ORD-LGA 3,227; LAX-JFK 3,433 (S03 slides p.14)
US autos 2025 all firms: GM 18, Toyota 16, Ford 14, Hyundai/Kia 11; C4 59%, HHI 2,578. Domestic only: GM 50, Ford 39, Tesla 10, Rivian 1; C4 100%, HHI 4,122 (S03 slides p.15)
Change in avg top-4 share by sector 1997-2017: increasing lack of competition (S03 slides p.10)
Allegiant business model: low-cost, leisure-only, ~75% of routes no nonstop competition, ancillary $76.35/passenger in 2025 (S03 workbook Solution!B18)
usefulness: Useful in quantifying industry rivalry, degree of buyer, and supplier power (S03 p.10)
Used by the Justice Department when determining whether to approve a merger (S03 p.10)
C4 and HHI positively correlated; C4 uses top four firms, HHI uses all firms; HHI squares shares so it places greater weight on firms with larger shares (S03 p.11)
limitations: Do the relevant companies compete at a national, regional, or local level? (S03 p.17)
Do the measures account for foreign imports? (S03 p.17)
In what product segments do firms actually compete? (S03 p.17)
traps: Use shares as decimals before squaring (42% → 0.42), then ×10,000
Treat 'remaining share' as one firm only when told (professor's telecom convention)
C4 can be identical while HHI differs (telecom 2013 vs 2014: both 94%, HHI 3,154 vs 2,706)
National HHI understates route/local concentration

title: Industry Analysis

learningObjectives.text: Know and understand the following concepts: rivalry, substitute, barriers to entry, buyer power, supplier power, attractiveness of an industry, switching costs, backward integration, forward integration, network effects
learningObjectives.src: course-data.js Session 4 'Read: Chapter 2'; S04 slides p.11

learningObjectives.text: Know and understand how to correctly identify a firm's industries and markets
Be able to identify and evaluate the five major forces that shape average industry profitability to evaluate the overall attractiveness of an industry
Be able to identify the factors in the general environment that affect firm and industry profitability
Know and understand where to find information necessary to perform industry analysis

keyTerms.def: Competition between firms within the incumbent industry. Lower levels of rivalry tend to have a positive effect on industry profits.

The relative power of companies and/or consumers who purchase products or services from the incumbent industry. When buyers have a lot of power they negotiate for lower prices and/or other concessions. High buyer power makes the focus industry less attractive.
The relative power of firms who sell materials/products to the incumbent industry. High supplier power has a negative effect on the profitability of the incumbent industry.

keyTerms.term: Threat of new entrants / barriers to entry
keyTerms.def: The possibility of newcomers entering and capturing market share from incumbents. If barriers to entry are high, the threat of new entrants is low, making the industry more attractive for incumbents.

A product that customers could switch to that is not necessarily in direct rivalry with incumbents, e.g., driving instead of flying (Honda is not in direct rivalry with Delta). Fulfills the same job in a different way.
keyTerms.src: Five Forces Tool, Glossary!B47; S04 slides p.23

keyTerms.def: How hard it is for customers to switch from one incumbent's product to another. The harder it is, the more attractive the industry.
A buyer entering the incumbent industry and becoming its own supplier. The easier it is for buyers to backward integrate, the more power buyers have.
A supplier entering the incumbent industry. If it is easy for suppliers to forward integrate, suppliers have greater power relative to incumbents.
A product becomes more valuable to consumers as more consumers use it; strong network effects lower the threat of new entrants.
Evaluated from the incumbent's point of view; the five forces shape average industry profitability. Scored 1 (least) to 5 (most attractive) in the tool.
keyTerms.src: Five Forces Tool, Instructions!A2; S04 Solution

industryDefinition: Three ways: (1) 'What job are your customers hiring you to do?' test; (2) industry classifications (NAICS); (3) organizational self-descriptions (S04 slides p.13)

NAICS codes range from 2 to 6 digits; more digits = more narrowly defined industry. Netflix: 51 Information → 516210 Media Streaming Distribution Services... Before 2022 Netflix was 532282 Video Tape and Disc Rental; streaming overtook DVD-by-mail in 2011; classifications lag in dynamic industries (Skills: Defining a Company's Industry page)
Self-descriptions: About page and Item 1 (Business) of the 10-K (Skills page)
Home Depot & Lowe's: NAICS 444110 Home Centers (S04 slides p.15). Home Depot 10-K: 'world's largest home improvement retailer', 2,347 stores (S04 slides p.17)
Prof's conclusion: Netflix competes in the global streaming entertainment industry (Skills page)

rivalry: Who are the competitors in the industry?
Is the industry fragmented or concentrated?
Are products or services in the industry standardized?
Are switching costs in the industry high?
Does the industry have high fixed costs?
buyer: Who are the primary customers in the industry? How many are there?
Are buyers in the industry price sensitive?
Are the industry's products a significant proportion of the buyer's costs?
Do buyers purchase in large volumes?
Do the industry's products affect buyers' performance?
Do the industry's products save buyers money?
supplier: Who are the primary suppliers in the industry? How many are there?
entry: Do economies of scale, experience, or learning exist in the industry?
Are patents or proprietary technology important for this industry?
Do industry incumbents have preferential access to critical resources?
Does entry into the industry require high capital investments?
Are there network effects in the industry that deter entry?
Do government policies or regulations make it more difficult to enter?
substitutes: What are substitute products or services that fulfill the same job but do so in a different way?
Are customers aware of substitute products or services?
Are substitute products or services readily available?
Are substitute products or services more or less expensive than those offered in the focal industry?

workedExamples.name: S04 Solution: Storage & Warehouse Leasing (self-storage) Five Forces
workedExamples.answer: Rivalry 2.36 (moderately unattractive); Buyer power 3.33 (moderately attractive); Supplier power 4.78 (very attractive); Threat of entry 2.83 (moderately unattractive); Substitutes 3.40 (moderately attractive); Overall 3.34

workedExamples.name: Scoring mechanics
workedExamples.answer: Each component rated 1-5 (whole numbers). Force score = weighted average of component scores (weights col I); component with sub-components = weighted avg of sub-ratings (sub-weights col K). Overall = weighted avg of the five force scores. Bands: 1-2 very unattractive, 2-3 moderately unattractive, 3-4 moderately attractive, 4-5 very attractive.
workedExamples.src: S04 Solution, Calculations Hub!K21..K107; Five Forces!A23

debriefLessons: Growth rate: rate on the forward-looking rate (2026-31 CAGR -0.1%), not the trailing 2021-26 CAGR (+4.3%): 'industry analysis asks whether the industry will be attractive from now into the near future, not what growth has already been captured' (S04 Solution Five Forces!A15, A33, A85)

Buyer concentration: market SEGMENTS (long-term residential 52.5%) are not buyers; millions of households → top-4 buyers far below 40% → rating 5. 'Reading the 52.5% as a buyer concentration figure is the most common error on this component.' (S04 Solution!A29)
Profitability of average buyer: households don't earn a profit; 0-5% (S04 Solution!A44)
Reasoned judgement is acceptable when the report lacks data; note reasoning (Instructions!A21)
cases: Theory Meets Practice (WSJ Aug 30, 2025): Thompson Traders copper bathtubs & tariffs; Lowe's/Home Depot set retail price, agreed only to 4-5% increase — which party has leverage? Who eats the cost of tariffs? (buyer power) (S04 slides pp.8-10)

Meta 10-K Item 1A risk factors → PEST; reputation loss could increase rivalry, buyer power (advertisers), and substitutes; Aug 2026 update: $18B settlement with 48 state AGs, under-18 limits; last $5.3B contingent on TikTok/YouTube agreeing (Skills: Analyzing the General Environment page)

Most profitable industries 2015-2024 by ROIC: Internet Software & Services 33%; Interactive Media 27%; Software 22%; Specialty Retail 19% (Home Depot, Lowe's, Best Buy); Household Products 17%. Least: Tech Hardware -9%; Insurance 1%; Banks 2%; Energy Equipment 2%; Office REITs 3% (S04 slides pp.27-28)
Neighbor, 'the Airbnb of storage' (videos) — a substitute/new entrant for self-storage (S04 module)
IBISWorld industry reports as a data source (S04 slides p.24; IBISWorld 44411 report)

pest.def: Political, Economic, Social, Technological trends in the general environment that may alter one or more of the five forces and industry attractiveness. Identify them via 10-K Item 1A Risk Factors.
pest.src: Skills: Analyzing the General Environment page

traps: Ratings run 1 = least attractive to 5 = most attractive for incumbents — high buyer power → LOW rating
Segments ≠ buyers when rating buyer concentration
Use forward-looking growth rates
Substitutes do the same job a different way; rivals do the same job the same way

keyTerms.def: A quantitative formula that defines the relationship between a set of inputs and outputs.
The rise over the run, or the change in y over the change in x (Δy/Δx). For y = mx + b, m is the slope and b is the intercept.

A function that evaluates the instantaneous rate of change of some original function, i.e., it tells you the slope (Δy/Δx) at any given value of x. For a straight line, the slope and derivative are equal; for a curve, it is the slope of the tangent line at that point.
keyTerms.src: Math Review p.5; S05 slides pp.19-20

keyTerms.def: For y = x^a, dy/dx = a·x^(a−1). Bring the exponent down in front and subtract 1 from the exponent; constants (no x) drop out.
keyTerms.src: Math Review p.5; S05 slides p.27

keyTerms.def: The derivative of a function with respect to one individual independent variable while the other variables are held constant. Written ∂y/∂x. Used to isolate the effect of specific variables.
keyTerms.src: Math Review p.10; S05 slides p.43

title: Cost & Economies of Scale

learningObjectives.text: Know and understand the sources of cost advantage

Know and understand the following economic concepts and how they relate to one another: fixed costs, variable costs, total cost, average fixed cost, average variable cost, average total cost, marginal cost, economies of scale
Understand the strategic implications of economies of scale (i.e., when does it make sense to grow?)

keyTerms.def: Defines the relationship between production (Q) and total cost (C). Total cost can be broken into fixed (FC) and variable costs (VC).
The part of the cost function that does not change with Q (the constant term).
keyTerms.src: S06 Video Slides p.14; CQ3 Q1 feedback

keyTerms.def: Every term that changes with Q.
keyTerms.src: S06 Video Slides p.15; CQ3 Q2 feedback

keyTerms.def: AFC = FC/Q
AVC = VC(Q)/Q
ATC = AVC + AFC (= C/Q)
The cost of producing an additional unit of output, or the change in cost attributable to the last unit of output. MC = ΔC/ΔQ = dC/dQ.
In the short run, capital (e.g., number of grills) is fixed and labor is variable; in the long run a manager is free to adjust all inputs — all costs are variable.
Defines the minimum average cost of producing alternative levels of output, allowing for optimal selection of fixed and variable factors of production.
Exist when long-run average costs decline as output is increased.
Exist when long-run average costs rise as output is increased.
'Practice makes perfect': firms become more efficient through practice; costs fall with cumulative output over time, whereas economies of scale come from the volume produced in a given period.
Cost per unit (y) plotted against scale (x), fit with a power function y = a·x^b. Slope of the curve = 2^b = cost multiplier per doubling; % drop per doubling = 1 − 2^b.
keyTerms.src: S06 workbook Solution!B49-E84; Cost Advantage Part 1 step 5

formulas.name: DuPont

cases: Competing on cost (S06 slides p.7): Kroger competes on cost (keeps 21¢ of each sales dollar after groceries vs. Whole Foods 36¢); Whole Foods on differentiation (premium covers overhead of 29% vs. Kroger's 18%); Kroger wins on volume ($3.50 sales per $ assets vs. $2.50); Safeway is stuck in the middle (1.5% operating margin; Albertsons bought it a year later); most successful in 2014: Whole Foods — best margins and ROA; Kroger's higher ROE comes mostly from debt.

HSIA Wars: Guest-Tek offered HSIA at $0.10 per room per day (early 2007); iBahn earned ~$0.65 on fixed-fee contracts; iBahn ~200,000 rooms, Guest-Tek ~500,000 after GoldenTree; ~2.5M rooms excluding 5-star; iBahn differentiated on security/VPN and 7-minute support calls (HSIA Wars case pp.1-3)

Guest-Tek verdict: can afford $0.10 since MC at current volume ≈ $0.10; but to cover fixed costs at that price they'd need ~2.2M rooms ≈ 88% of 2.5M select-service rooms; the competitor had a quality differentiator and scope economies, so Guest-Tek risked a price war it couldn't win (S06 workbook Solution!A112-A153)

Netflix vs. Redbox (Cost Advantage assignment): Redbox ATC per rental = 656.06·R^−0.476 (TC = 656.06·R^0.524); Netflix CPSPM = 38.10·S^−0.182; Redbox cost falls ~28.1% per doubling vs. Netflix ~11.9%; Netflix MCPEH ≈ $0.096/hr vs. Redbox ≈ $0.65/hr in 2016-2 (Kimball's Cost Advantage workbook — his answers, not an official key)
'Scale economies work in reverse': Redbox's rentals were shrinking, moving it UP its steep scale curve (Kimball's Cost Advantage Part 1 step 6)
traps: MC excludes fixed costs (marginal cost is only the variable cost of the last unit)
MC crosses AVC and ATC at their minimum points
ATC − AVC = AFC, which shrinks toward zero as Q rises
Units: Guest-Tek costs are in $000s; convert rooms to room-days (×365/4)
Learning/experience = cumulative output over time; scale = volume in a period
Video slide p.16 prints 'C = 8 + 58 = $58' — the correct arithmetic is 8 + 50 = $58

title: Demand & Consumer Surplus

learningObjectives.text: Know and understand the following concepts: market demand curve, law of demand, change in quantity demanded, shift in demand, normal good, inferior good, substitute, complement, demand function, inverse demand function, consumer surplus
Know and understand how to construct and plot a demand curve
Know how to calculate the revenue maximizing price using calculus
Know how to calculate consumer surplus and describe what it means
Know and understand the four major categories or sources of product or service differentiation
learningObjectives.src: course-data.js Session 7 (taught in the 'Differentiation Advantage' LearnStrategy video — transcript not in materials)

keyTerms.def: Shows the total quantity of a good that all consumers in the market would purchase at each price, holding other factors constant.
Price and quantity demanded are inversely related: a price increase leads to a decrease in quantity demanded (and vice versa), all else equal.
keyTerms.src: S08 slides p.16 (applied); GENERAL ECON wording

keyTerms.def: A movement ALONG a demand curve caused by a change in the good's own price.
The whole curve moves (left = decrease, right = increase) because a non-price determinant changed: income, prices of related goods, advertising/consumer tastes, population, expectations.
keyTerms.src: GENERAL ECON (B&P Ch 2 topic); determinants listed in S05 slides p.41 and Math Review p.9

keyTerms.def: Demand increases when income rises; the coefficient on income in a demand function is positive.
keyTerms.src: CQ4 Q2 feedback (sign logic); Regression Exercise step 6 (Kimball)

keyTerms.def: Demand decreases when income rises; the coefficient on income is negative.
An increase in the price of good y raises demand for good x; the coefficient on Py is positive (CPE > 0).
keyTerms.src: CQ4 Q1 feedback; S08 slides p.27, p.29

keyTerms.def: An increase in the price of good y lowers demand for good x; the coefficient on Py is negative (CPE < 0), e.g., milk and cereal.
Quantity as a function of price (and other variables), e.g., Qx = 10,000 − 4Px + 5Py − 0.2I.
Price on the left, as a function of quantity: solve the demand function for P. E.g., Qx = 4,500 − 4Px → Px = 1,125 − 0.25Qx.
The area under the demand curve and above the price: the value consumers receive beyond what they pay. For linear demand, a triangle = ½ × quantity × (choke price − price).
keyTerms.src: CQ4 Q4 feedback; meaning = GENERAL ECON

keyTerms.def: The price where quantity demanded hits zero (the vertical intercept of demand).

title: Elasticity & Price Discrimination

learningObjectives.text: Know and understand the following concepts: own price elasticity, inelastic and elastic demand, the total revenue test, cross price elasticity
Know how to calculate the various forms of elasticity and understand how they relate to strategy

keyTerms.def: A measure of responsiveness of one variable to changes in another variable; the percentage change in one variable relative to changes in another; a measure of sensitivity (e.g., price-sensitive customers).
OPE = %ΔQx/%ΔPx = (∂Qx/∂Px)(Px/Qx). OPE will always be negative (law of demand).
OPE < −1. Consumers are relatively price sensitive.
−1 < OPE < 0. Consumers are relatively price insensitive.
OPE = −1.

(1) If demand is elastic (OPE < −1), a price increase (decrease) leads to a decrease (increase) in total revenue. (2) If inelastic (−1 < OPE < 0), a price increase (decrease) leads to an increase (decrease) in total revenue. (3) Total revenue is maximized when demand is unitary elastic.
CPE = %ΔQx/%ΔPy = (∂Qx/∂Py)(Py/Qx). Can be negative or positive: positive → substitutes (Dr Pepper vs. Mr. Pibb); negative → complements (milk and cereal).
%ΔQx/%ΔI; positive for normal goods, negative for inferior goods.

title: Forecasting Demand Using Linear Regression

learningObjectives.text: Know and understand the following statistical terms: regression coefficient, standard error, t-statistic, p-value, R-squared
Know how to run a regression model in Excel
Know and understand how to interpret and use regression output

keyTerms.def: The line that minimizes the sum of squared deviations between the line and the actual data points. Y = a + bX, where a and b are parameters that define the intercept and slope. Objective: estimate the parameters that define the true relationship between Y and X(s).

Estimates of the true parameters that define the relationship between dependent and independent variables. Interpretation: 'A one-unit increase in x leads to (magnitude of coefficient) increase/decrease (sign of coefficient) in y.'
The standard deviation of the parameter estimate; a measure of how noisy our estimate is. The smaller/greater the standard error, the more/less precise your parameter estimate.

The ratio of the parameter estimate (regression coefficient) to its standard error. Generally, t-statistics greater than 2 in absolute value indicate the coefficient is statistically significant (not equal to zero).

An alternative measure of statistical significance; per the slides, it 'tells you the probability that a true parameter that you estimated is equal to zero.' By convention, a coefficient is statistically significant when its p-value is less than 0.05.

Coefficient of determination; a measure of model fit equal to explained variation over total variation; ranges from 0 to 1. 'An R-squared of ___ indicates that ___% of the variation in y can be explained by variation in the x's.'
Square root of R-squared.
R-squared penalized for the number of variables the model uses.
Multiple regression isolates the effect of one variable holding others constant (the airline fare example; Netflix growth and season removed).

title: Profit Maximization Across Market Structures

learningObjectives.text: Know and understand the following economic terms: marginal analysis, marginal benefit, marginal cost, marginal revenue, monopoly, monopolistic competition, perfectly competitive market
Be able to identify when a firm operates in an industry that is perfectly competitive, monopolistically competitive, or a monopoly
Be able to identify the sources of (and strategies for obtaining) monopoly power
Know how to calculate the profit-maximizing levels of price and quantity for perfectly competitive, monopolistically competitive, and monopoly firms using marginal analysis

keyTerms.def: Deciding by comparing the benefit and cost of one more unit: keep going until the marginal benefit (MB) equals the marginal cost (MC). MB = MC.
The additional benefit (e.g., revenue) from one more unit of an activity.
keyTerms.src: S10 slides p.15 (table); wording GENERAL ECON

keyTerms.def: The additional cost of one more unit (dC/dQ).
keyTerms.src: S06 Video p.20; S10 slides p.15

keyTerms.def: The additional revenue collected when one additional unit of production or service is rendered. MR = dR/dQ.

Many firms; homogeneous goods (commodities); perfect information: yes; transaction costs: no; free entry/exit: yes; no influence on price (price taker); D_firm = P_market = MR; Q* where P_market = MC(Q*); P* = P_market.
Many firms; differentiated goods (fast food); perfect information: no; transaction costs: yes; free entry/exit: yes; price maker; faces its own D_firm; Q* where MR(Q*) = MC(Q*); P* = P(Q*).
One firm (e.g., rural gas station); price maker; D_firm = D_market; Q* where MR(Q*) = MC(Q*); P* = P(Q*). Information, transaction costs, entry: N/A in the professor's table.
A price taker has no influence on price (perfect competition); a price maker sets price from its downward-sloping demand (monopoly, monopolistic competition).

title: Advanced Pricing Strategies

learningObjectives.text: Know and understand price discrimination, two-part pricing, block pricing, commodity bundling, and peak-load pricing
Know and understand the three forms of price discrimination
Know how to calculate the profit-maximizing price when using two-part pricing, block pricing, commodity bundling, and peak-load pricing
Be able to articulate the benefits and risks of charging different prices to different customers
Know how to calculate consumer surplus and describe what it means

status: Rebuilt from S11 Slides - Advanced Pricing Strategies.pdf and the Cascade Heating & Air exercise. The slide objective also names cross-subsidies; the deck does not define or calculate one.

keyTerms.def: Charging different prices to different consumers (or for different units) for the same good, where the price differences are not due to cost differences.
Charging each consumer the maximum they are willing to pay for each unit; the firm captures all consumer surplus.
Charging a per-unit price that depends on how many units are bought (e.g., quantity discounts); consumers self-select.
Charging different groups (with different, identifiable elasticities) different prices, e.g., student or senior discounts. Charge the higher price to the less elastic group.
A fixed fee for the right to buy plus a per-unit price. Profit-maximizing: set per-unit price = MC and the fixed fee = the consumer surplus each consumer receives at that price.
Selling identical units only in a package (block); the profit-maximizing package price equals the total value (area under demand) of the package quantity, where package quantity is where P = MC.
Selling two or more different products together for a single price; profitable when consumers' reservation prices are negatively correlated and the firm cannot price discriminate.
Charging a higher price during peak demand (when capacity is constrained and MC is high) and a lower price off-peak. Set P where MR = MC in each period.
Pricing one product below cost (or low) to boost demand for a complementary product that earns the profit (e.g., cheap printers, profitable ink).

Setting the internal price at which an upstream division sells an input to a downstream division of the same firm; to maximize overall firm profit (no external market), set the transfer price equal to the upstream division's marginal cost.

formulas.latex: \text{Package price} = MC\cdot Q + CS \text{ at } P=MC
